accroche: In The Theory of the Leisure Class (1899), Veblen calls an expenditure “waste,” and specifies that the word is not an insult.
contenu_vulgarise:
A sumptuous dinner, a watch whose price far exceeds its usefulness, an outfit that serves only to be seen: we readily read vanity into these. In 1899, the American economist Thorstein Veblen publishes *The Theory of the Leisure Class* and proposes another reading. For him, these expenditures do not betray a whim: they do social work.

## The Mechanism

The starting point is a sentence from the book: it is not enough to possess wealth or power, they must be put in evidence, for esteem is awarded only on evidence. In the societies Veblen describes, the first proof is abstention from work: visible leisure becomes the conventional mark of superior pecuniary achievement.

When fortune grows, leisure is no longer enough. Veblen writes that conspicuous consumption of valuable goods is a means of reputability for the man of leisure. As his wealth accumulates, his own efforts no longer suffice to make it visible. He therefore recruits his friends and his competitors: expensive gifts, feasts, and costly entertainments serve as witnesses to the expenditure.

Veblen calls this expenditure “waste,” and takes care to defuse the word. He uses it because this expenditure does not serve, in his view, human life or human well-being taken as a whole. But from the consumer's point of view, he writes, the question of waste does not arise in economic theory: everyone obtains what they prefer. Used as a technical term, the word therefore implies no reproach of the motives of the one who spends. The reproach, Veblen adds, comes from everyday language.

## What It Shifts

If the expenditure serves as proof, its price is part of the message. Drawing the consequence, an identical but cheap good would not provide the same proof: part of what one buys is what others can read in it.

Veblen does not, however, denounce individual failings. Good manners and refined ways of life are, he writes, items of conformity to the norm of conspicuous leisure and consumption: he describes a norm of reputation, which separates his text from a sermon against luxury.

One question remains that the book poses without closing: what, in a society, decides what counts as proof?

citation.texte: Conspicuous consumption of valuable goods is a means of reputability to the gentleman of leisure.
citation.source: The Theory of the Leisure Class, ch. IV, 1899

carte.punch: Veblen calls an expenditure “waste,” without the slightest reproach.
carte.idee: For Veblen (1899), visible luxury serves as proof of wealth, since esteem is awarded only on evidence. He uses “waste” as a technical term, without blaming those who spend: the price is part of the message.

quiz.question: Why does Veblen call conspicuous consumption “waste”?
choix: Because he judges the rich who spend without counting to be morally guilty
Because this expenditure, in his view, does not serve human well-being as a whole, without blaming anyone
Because luxury goods deteriorate faster than the ordinary goods of the time
Because these sumptuary expenditures were always forbidden by law in his day
quiz.explication: Veblen specifies that the word is a technical term: it does not target the consumer's motives, since the consumer obtains what he prefers. He speaks neither of morality, nor of the durability of goods, nor of legality; the reproach, he writes, comes from everyday language.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Veblen, what is the first conventional proof of pecuniary success, before conspicuous consumption takes over?
choix: The ownership of farmland passed down from generation to generation
Abstention from work, visible leisure having become the conventional mark of superiority
The number of servants employed year-round
Regular attendance at a private club
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Veblen puts abstention from work first, visible leisure becoming the conventional mark of superior pecuniary achievement, before wealth grows further.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Veblen, why does the wealthy man recruit his friends and competitors around expensive gifts and feasts?
choix: To comply with a legal obligation of redistribution
To escape the wealth tax in force in his day
Because the law requires him to organize public events
Because his own efforts no longer suffice to make his wealth visible, and he needs witnesses to the expenditure
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Veblen explains that as fortune accumulates, the wealthy man's efforts alone no longer suffice to make it visible, so he recruits witnesses through expensive gifts, feasts, and entertainments.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Veblen say about good manners and refined ways of life?
choix: That they are items of conformity to the norm of conspicuous leisure and consumption
That they have no relation to the leisure class he describes
That they will disappear with industrialization, according to his forecast
That they are reserved for the poorest classes of the society he observes
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Veblen writes that good manners and refined ways of life are items of conformity to the norm of conspicuous leisure and consumption, not virtues isolated from their bearers.
